summary: Describes the flow and service information model for Deterministic Networking, defined for IP and MPLS DetNet data planes. It provides a common way to describe flows and the services they need.

plainLanguage.summary: Deterministic Networking (DetNet) carries specific data streams for real-time applications with very little packet loss and a guaranteed maximum delivery time. RFC 9016 defines the words used to describe such a stream: how to recognize its packets, how much traffic it will send, and what the network must promise for it. It defines what to record, not how to configure the routers.

questions: what information describes a detnet flow
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for describing deterministic network flows and the guarantees they need.

tldr.problem: Applications that need a guaranteed maximum delay and a very low packet loss rate must describe what they need in a way the network operator can act on.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9016 defines an information model with three groups of parameters: App-flow parameters for the application data, DetNet flow parameters for the flow as the network carries it, and DetNet service parameters for the guarantees the network offers.
tldr.outcome: Operators, users and implementors get one vocabulary for Deterministic Networking over IP and MPLS, aligned with IEEE 802.1 TSN and used as input to the DetNet YANG model.

facts.label: IP flow identifier
facts.value: 6-tuple: source IP, destination IP, DSCP, protocol, source port, destination port

today: RFC 9016 is an Informational RFC published in March 2021 and has not been obsoleted. It remains the description of the DetNet flow and service information models; the machine-readable YANG model is a separate document.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Deterministic Networking (DetNet) carries specified unicast or multicast data flows for real-time applications with extremely low packet loss rates and assured maximum end-to-end delivery latency. RFC 9016 describes the flow and service information models that users, operators and implementors use to understand and configure such a service. The background and concepts of DetNet are in RFC 8655.

The document separates three kinds of model. Flow information models describe the characteristics of a data flow. Service information models describe the service provided for data flows, and are independent of any one network operator. Configuration information models describe the settings a network node needs. Flow and service models are exchanged between the user and the network operator; configuration models are exchanged between the management or control plane and the network nodes.

The scope is narrow on purpose. This document specifies flow and service information models only. It does not specify flow data models or DetNet configuration, and the DetNet-specific YANG data model lives in a separate document. The information model is based on the DetNet architecture in RFC 8655 and on the data model of IEEE 802.1Qcc, so that the same descriptions work for Layer 2 and Layer 3 network segments.
sections.plainLanguage: DetNet is a way to move specific data streams for real-time applications, with very few lost packets and a guaranteed maximum delivery time. This RFC sets out what to write down about such a stream so that the application owner and the network operator describe it in the same terms.

sections.title: Three Groups of Information Elements
sections.content:
The model rests on three groups of information. App-flow-related parameters describe the application traffic itself: a unique FlowID, the FlowType (Ethernet, MPLS or IP), a DataFlowSpecification that says which packets belong to the flow, a TrafficSpecification, the FlowEndpoints, a FlowStatus and a FlowRank. A second App-flow parameter, FlowRequirements, states what the application needs in terms of bandwidth, latency, latency variation, loss and misordering tolerance.

DetNet flow-related parameters describe the flow as the network carries it: DnFlowID, DnPayloadType, DnFlowFormat (MPLS or IP), DnFlowSpecification, DnTrafficSpecification, DnFlowEndpoints, DnFlowRank, DnFlowStatus, plus DnFlowRequirements and DnFlowBiDir.

DetNet service-related parameters describe the service the network offers: DnServiceID, DnServiceDeliveryType, the DnServiceDeliveryProfile with its bandwidth, latency and loss limits, connectivity type (point-to-point or point-to-multipoint), DnServiceBiDir, DnServiceRank and DnServiceStatus.

The mapping between them is many-to-one in one direction. One DetNet flow contains one or more aggregated App-flows, and one DetNet service carries one or more DetNet flows.
sections.plainLanguage: The model has three lists. One describes the application data before the network touches it. One describes the flow after the network has wrapped it in its own headers. One describes the service the network promises. A single service can carry several flows, and a single flow can bundle several application streams.

sections.title: Identifying a DetNet Flow
sections.content:
The network recognizes a flow by looking at header fields in the packets it forwards. For an MPLS DetNet flow the identifiers are the MPLS context: the SLabel and the FLabelStack. For an IP DetNet flow the identifiers are a 6-tuple made up of the source IP address, the destination IP address, the DSCP value, the protocol number, the source port and the destination port. Two further attributes can be used in addition to that 6-tuple: the IPv6 flow label and the IPsec SPI. The RFC notes that the 6-tuple and the use of wildcards for these attributes are specified in RFC 8939.

The model also fixes reference points. An App-flow starts at its Source and ends at its Destination. A DetNet flow starts at its DN Ingress and ends at its DN Egress, and these two points sit in the middle of the served App-flow. A DN Ingress may add the encapsulation the technology needs, such as MPLS labels, UDP or IP headers, and a DN Egress may remove it again. All reference points in this document are packet-based.
sections.plainLanguage: To know which packets belong to a flow, the network reads their headers. In an MPLS network it reads the label stack. In an IP network it reads the two addresses, the DSCP value, the protocol number and the two port numbers. The point where the network takes the flow in is called the ingress; the point where it hands it over is the egress.

sections.title: Traffic Specification
sections.content:
DnTrafficSpecification says how the DN Ingress will transmit packets for the flow. It is the promise the ingress makes to the network, and the network uses it to allocate resources and to adjust queue parameters in its nodes.

It has five attributes. Interval is the period of time the specification applies to, given as an integer number of nanoseconds. MaxPacketsPerInterval and MinPacketsPerInterval bound the number of packets sent in one interval. MaxPayloadSize and MinPayloadSize bound the payload size in octets. Together they can describe constant bitrate traffic and variable bitrate traffic, and they can be used to represent worst-case scenarios during resource allocation.

Traffic that exceeds the specification may get different network behaviour from the one the network was engineered for. Excess traffic caused by a malicious or malfunctioning device can be prevented or mitigated with existing mechanisms such as policing and shaping. When MinPayloadSize and MinPacketsPerInterval are used, packets smaller than MinPayloadSize count as MinPayloadSize while packet size matters, such as during policing, and flows below MinPacketsPerInterval count as MinPacketsPerInterval during resource reservation.
sections.plainLanguage: This part states how much traffic the source promises to send: how many packets per interval, how big those packets are, and how long the interval is. The network reserves capacity and sets its queues from those numbers. Traffic that stays within the promise gets the behaviour the network was built for.

sections.title: Flow Requirements and Rank
sections.content:
DnFlowRequirements holds six limits that together describe the service level the flow needs. MinBandwidth is the minimum bandwidth that must be guaranteed, in octets per second. MaxLatency is the maximum time from ingress to egress for a single packet, as an integer number of nanoseconds. MaxLatencyVariation is the difference between the minimum and the maximum one-way end-to-end latency, also in nanoseconds. MaxLoss gives the maximum packet loss rate requirement between ingress and egress, together with the interval over which the loss is measured.

MaxConsecutiveLossTolerance is the maximum number of consecutive packets whose loss the application tolerates, which can be measured for example from sequence numbers. MaxMisordering is the largest number of packets that may be received out of order; a value of zero means in-order delivery is required and no misordering can be tolerated. When a packet arrives at the egress after one with a higher sequence number, the difference between the sequence number values cannot be bigger than MaxMisordering plus one.

DnFlowRank gives the flow a position relative to other flows in the DetNet domain. The range is 0 to 255 and the value 0 is the highest priority. The domain uses the rank to decide which flows can be bumped, meaning removed from the node configuration, when resources run out, for example when a port becomes oversubscribed after a network reconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the promises the application asks for: enough bandwidth, a time limit for each packet, a limit on how much that time varies, an acceptable loss rate, and whether packets may arrive out of order. Every flow also gets a priority number from 0 to 255, where 0 is the most important, so that the network knows which flow to give up first when it runs short of capacity.

sections.title: Joining, Leaving and Modifying a Flow
sections.content:
Three information groups carry flow-specific information. DnIngress and DnEgress specify the source and the destination of a single DetNet flow and travel from the user of the service to the network. DnFlowStatus travels back from the network to the user and says whether the flow is ready to use.

Status is reported separately for the ingress and the egress. Both can be None (no such point), Ready, Failed or OutOfService (administratively blocked). The egress adds PartialFailed, meaning one or more egresses are ready and one or more have failed; the flow can still be used if the ingress is Ready. A nonzero FailureCode says what went wrong, for example that packet replication and elimination was requested but is not possible.

There are three operations. Join means an ingress or egress intends to join the flow and carries DnFlowSpecification, DnFlowRank, DnFlowEndpoint and DnTrafficSpecification, with the service requirements group optional. Leave means the point intends to leave the flow and carries DnFlowSpecification and DnFlowEndpoint. Modify carries the same fields as Join and covers small changes, for example only MaxPayloadSize changing. The reason Modify exists is that it lets a change begin while the current flow keeps running until the change is accepted. Without a link between the Join and the Leave, a controller working out whether the new specification can be supported has to assume the resources committed to the current flow are still in use. The RFC calls Modify optional, because of possible controller plane limitations.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow joins the network when an endpoint says it wants to be part of it, and leaves when it no longer wants to be. A third operation, Modify, asks for a small change to a running flow, such as a different maximum packet size, without taking the flow down first. The network also reports back whether the flow works, and if it fails, why.

viz.caption: THE SIX FLOW REQUIREMENT PARAMETERS AND THEIR UNITS

items.label: Minimum bandwidth
items.desc: Minimum bandwidth that must be guaranteed, in octets per second.

items.label: Maximum latency
items.desc: Maximum ingress to egress time for a single packet, in nanoseconds.

items.label: Maximum latency variation
items.desc: Difference between the minimum and the maximum one-way latency, in nanoseconds.

items.label: Maximum loss
items.desc: Maximum packet loss rate between ingress and egress, with its measurement interval.

items.label: Maximum consecutive loss
items.desc: Maximum number of consecutive packets whose loss the application tolerates.

items.label: Maximum misordering
items.desc: Largest number of packets that may be received out of order; zero requires in-order delivery.

items.label: No ingress or egress
items.desc: There is no such reference point for this flow.

items.label: Ready
items.desc: The ingress is ready, or all egresses are ready.

items.label: Failed
items.desc: The ingress failed, or all egresses failed.

items.label: Partially failed
items.desc: One or more egresses are ready and one or more failed; the flow can be used if the ingress is Ready.

items.label: Administratively blocked
items.desc: The point is blocked on purpose.
